messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 24
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 33

At 24, she works the early shift at a regional warehouse, scanning pallets and moving boxed merchandise from one conveyor line to another. She likes the predictability of the job: the hum of the belts, the handheld scanner beeping in her palm, the clear beginning and end of each task. Before the bombing, she says, she was the kind of person who could joke through a long shift, stop for coffee with coworkers afterward, and call her mother on the bus ride home. She was careful, but not frightened. She moved through the city with the ordinary confidence of someone who expected to arrive where she was going.

The attack happens on a Saturday afternoon nearly a year ago. She is downtown meeting a cousin for lunch in a crowded market district, a place full of music, tourists, and food carts. She remembers standing in line for an arepa, scrolling through a message on her phone, when a blast cracks through the street. At first she does not understand what she is hearing. Then the air changes. She feels pressure in her chest and ears, followed by screaming, the metallic smell of smoke, and a rain of dust and shattered glass. People begin running in all directions. Someone slams into her shoulder hard enough to knock her to the ground. For a few seconds, she cannot find her breath. She thinks, very clearly, I am going to die here.

When she gets up, her knees are shaking so badly she can barely stand. Her cousin is not beside her anymore. She starts calling her name, but her own voice sounds thin and far away. There is blood on a stranger’s shirt. A stroller lies overturned near the curb. Sirens start almost immediately, then seem to multiply until they fill everything. She remembers hiding behind a concrete planter with several other people, her body folded inward, her phone slipping in her hand because of sweat. Even after she learns her cousin is alive and has escaped down another block, she cannot stop trembling. That night, safe at home, she sits on the bathroom floor and jumps at every sound from the street.

In the weeks after, everyone tells her how lucky she is. She says thank you because she knows that is what people mean when they are trying to comfort her. But inside, “lucky” feels like a word meant for someone else. She stops taking the bus downtown. She changes her route to work to avoid crowded terminals and refuses invitations to festivals or public events. At the warehouse, the crash of a dropped box sends a jolt through her whole body before she can think. Once, when a forklift backfires near loading bay three, she ducks instinctively and covers her head. Her coworkers laugh at first, assuming she is joking, and she laughs too, a second too late, her face burning with embarrassment.

Sleep becomes unreliable. Some nights she cannot fall asleep because she keeps replaying the moment before the explosion, trying to identify what she missed, as if vigilance now could undo what happened then. Other nights she wakes gasping from dreams in which she is back in the market, unable to move her legs while everyone else runs. In the morning she drags herself to her shift with a headache and a stomach that feels sour. She drinks more caffeine than she used to just to stay focused on inventory numbers. Even so, her mind slips. She scans the same label twice, forgets simple instructions, startles when someone approaches from behind. She begins choosing stations near the wall so she can keep the room in view.

Her family notices that she has changed before she is ready to admit it. She visits less often because her relatives are loud and affectionate and gather in crowded apartments where children race through the rooms shrieking. Sounds that once meant warmth now scrape at her nerves. Her mother tells her she seems distant. Her younger brother says she is always “somewhere else.” She wants to explain that being around people no longer feels simple, that part of her is always measuring exits, listening for anything unusual, preparing for danger before there is any proof of it. But when she tries to talk about the bombing, her throat tightens and she says only that work has been tiring.

What troubles her most is how unfamiliar she feels to herself. She used to think of herself as independent, steady, the person others leaned on. Now she catches her reflection in the dark screen of the scanner during quiet moments at work and sees someone braced for impact. On her days off, she tells herself she should go out, answer messages, live normally. Instead she stays in her apartment with the television on low for company, flinching if a news alert mentions an attack anywhere in the world. She keeps checking the lock on her door before bed, then checking it again. She knows the market is over, that she survived, that she is standing in a warehouse on an ordinary Tuesday. Her body does not seem to believe it.
